name: QANDA (Mathpresso Inc.)
origin_region: South Korea (Mathpresso Inc., Seoul); operates globally in 50+ countries, with Indonesia as one of its largest overseas markets alongside Vietnam, Japan and Thailand. Over 80-90% of cumulative users are outside Korea.
target_age: K-12 broadly (SD through SMA / elementary through high school). App Store age rating is 4+, but the product's real center of gravity is SMP-SMA (junior/senior high) homework, since the core loop is scanning a printed textbook problem. Indonesian press describes the user base as 'mulai SD sampai SMA'. An Indonesian academic evaluation specifically assessed its fitness for SD (elementary) self-study.
delivery_mode: online-app (Android/iOS, mobile-first, no offline/physical component). Adjacent paid services add live human tutoring (QANDA Tutor, 1:1 tablet-based) and B2B/B2G platforms (QANDA Math Coach, AIDT AI digital textbooks), but the mass-market Indonesia product is the free/freemium self-serve app.
language_localization: Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia) is a supported UI language — the App Store lists Indonesian among 14 languages (English, French, German, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Malay, Russian, Spanish, Thai, Traditional Chinese, Turkish, Vietnamese). Step-by-step solution text and the AI chat respond in Indonesian. Parent-facing reports are not localized because no parent-facing reporting layer exists in the consumer app.
pricing_model: freemium with a coin/credit economy plus subscription tiers. Free tier gives limited scans/answers; coins are consumed per search and can be earned free via referrals and events. Indonesian sources cite roughly Rp23,000/month for a 7,500-coin membership. App Store in-app purchases range $0.99 (extra coins) / $1.29 (ad-free) / $1.99 (basic) / $3.99-$16.49 (premium and pro tiers). [uncertain]
local_curriculum_alignment: No evidence of formal alignment to Kurikulum Merdeka or K13. QANDA's answer engine is built on a global crowdsourced/OCR-indexed question database plus an LLM (MathGPT), not on an Indonesian curriculum scope-and-sequence. It is reactive to whatever problem the student photographs, so alignment is incidental — the student's own school worksheet supplies the curriculum, not the app. No Kemendikbud partnership or Merdeka mapping was found in official Mathpresso materials.
does_error_type_diagnosis: no — this is the single most important finding for the gap analysis. QANDA diagnoses nothing about the child's reasoning; it recognizes and solves the PROBLEM, not the child's WORK. The OCR pipeline reads the printed question from a photo and returns a model solution. The child's own handwritten attempt, working steps, and crossed-out lines are never captured or analyzed, so there is no substrate from which an error type (misreading / conceptual / computational) could be inferred. The closest adjacent feature is the 'incorrect-answer notebook' (buku catatan salah), which is a storage bin of problems the student got wrong — it records WHICH problems were missed, never WHY. Mathpresso's B2B/B2G product QANDA Math Coach does advertise a 'comprehensive knowledge graph' for assessing student progress, which is topic-level mastery mapping, still not an error-type taxonomy, and is not exposed in the Indonesian consumer app.
diagnosis_granularity: trouble-spot-quantity — the consumer app tracks which problems were answered incorrectly (incorrect-answer notebook) and can generate similar problems and concept quizzes off the same concept, which implies a topic tag but not a diagnosed misconception. The B2B QANDA Math Coach tier reaches topic-mastery-map granularity via its knowledge graph. Neither reaches mcq-distractor-mapped-misconception nor full-error-type-taxonomy. [uncertain]
diagnosis_input_modality: free-response-ocr, but critically the OCR is applied to the QUESTION not to the STUDENT'S ANSWER. This is an inverted use of OCR relative to a diagnostic product: QANDA scans printed/typeset problems to look up or generate a solution. There is no handwriting-stroke capture of the child's working, no MCQ distractor logging, no video-explained reasoning, and no self-report of confusion. A secondary modality exists via the AI chat, where a student can type what they did and be corrected conversationally, but that is unstructured, unlogged as a diagnosis, and depends entirely on the child volunteering their reasoning.
ai_tutor_diagnosis_reliability: No published validation against any ground-truth error-type labels — Mathpresso publishes benchmark claims for MathGPT's problem-solving accuracy, not for diagnostic accuracy, because diagnosis is not a claimed capability. Reported failure modes are of the solver, not the diagnoser: user and reviewer complaints cite occasional wrong answers, weaker performance on advanced/university-level and out-of-syllabus problems, and bugs. More importantly, the architecture is structurally exposed to the 'correct answer trap' documented in the AI-tutor literature — when a student reaches a right answer via flawed reasoning, systems that evaluate the final answer rather than the reasoning process are blind to the underlying misconception. QANDA is a pure answer-oriented system and therefore sits fully inside that blind spot. Related VLM research (DrawEduMath follow-up) further finds vision-language models underperform specifically on struggling students' work and misdiagnose their errors, which is the exact population and task an error-type diagnosis product must serve.
evidence_quote: Official App Store feature list for QANDA (Mathpresso Inc.): 'Snap a photo, chat with AI, understand better' — features enumerated are 'Step-by-step explanations', 'Concept quizzes', 'Similar problems', 'Incorrect-answer notebook', 'Formula calculator and QANDA Notes', 'Focus & break timers', 'Study groups with friends', 'AI Friends — Your Study Companions'. No error-type diagnosis, misconception analysis, or parent dashboard appears anywhere in the official listing. Mathpresso's own product page describes QANDA as OCR plus 'Autosolver and LLM-based AI tutor' delivering 'solutions within five seconds', with the diagnostic-sounding language ('comprehensive knowledge graph', 'sophisticated learning assessment system') reserved for the separate B2B QANDA Math Coach and QANDA Tutor products. Liputan6 (19 Nov 2020) quotes Mathpresso CEO Ray Lee positioning the app on the combination of instant AI search and human tutors: 'Saat ini, belum ada aplikasi edukasi lain yang mampu menggabungkan kedua fitur tersebut dengan sempurna seperti Qanda.'
how_parent_involved: none (effectively passive; parent is at most an off-app gatekeeper/payer). The official App Store and Google Play listings contain no parent dashboard, no parent account linking, and no progress report to a guardian. The product is designed for the child to use alone and unsupervised — which is precisely why Indonesian commentary frames parental involvement as an external duty rather than a product feature, advising parents to accompany and steer the child so QANDA is used as a learning aid and not as a shortcut for finding exam answers. NOTE ON A CONTRADICTORY SOURCE: several SEO blog articles (jetlearn.com) describe a 'QANDA parent app' with a 'Progress Dashboard', study goals, time limits, and weekly/monthly usage reports. These claims are not corroborated by any official Mathpresso source, App Store/Play listing, or press release, and the articles cite no primary source; they appear to be generated marketing content and should be treated as unverified. [uncertain]
ai_tutor_directly_to_child: yes — and this is a meaningful market signal. QANDA explicitly supports interactive AI chat with the student: in addition to photographing a question, the child can converse with QANDA AI to work through a problem, and can prompt it for follow-ups such as 'Make a similar question using this concept' to instantly receive a concept quiz. The LLM-based AI Tutor launched in beta in August 2023 and the app now ships 'AI Friends — Your Study Companions'. The entire interaction is child-to-AI with no adult in the loop and no adult visibility into the transcript. So the precedent for AI talking directly to an Indonesian child is already established at scale — the unmet need is not the channel but the diagnosis flowing through it.
key_finding: QANDA is proof of enormous Indonesian demand and simultaneously proof that the diagnosis layer is unbuilt. It has reached roughly 2.5 million Indonesian users (Mathpresso claim, Nov 2020, ~10% of smartphone-owning SD-SMA students) and briefly ranked #1-2 in Google Play Education in Indonesia, beating Ruangguru and Zenius — yet it answers questions rather than diagnosing children. Three concrete gaps follow. (1) DIAGNOSIS GAP: OCR is pointed at the printed problem, not at the child's handwritten working, so no error type can be inferred even in principle; the 'incorrect-answer notebook' captures which items were missed, never why. Diagnostic language ('knowledge graph', 'learning assessment') is confined to the B2B QANDA Math Coach and paid QANDA Tutor tiers, absent from the mass-market Indonesian app. (2) PARENT GAP: there is no parent-facing surface at all in the consumer product — no dashboard, no report, no account linking — which for an SD-age child (whose parent is the payer, device owner, and decision-maker) is a structural omission rather than a minor one, and it is exactly why Indonesian coverage treats supervision as a parental chore imposed from outside the app. (3) MISUSE RISK AS OPPORTUNITY: Indonesian academic and journalistic sources converge on the concern that instant-answer AI reduces critical thinking, encourages plagiarism and dependence on instant answers, and makes it hard for teachers to verify authentic work — a failure mode that an error-type-diagnosis product structurally avoids, since diagnosing how a child went wrong requires the child to have actually attempted the work. QANDA is therefore best read as the incumbent that validates the market and defines the gap: massive distribution, real AI-to-child conversation, zero error-type diagnosis, zero parent role.
study_scale_or_sample: Company-reported scale (not independent audit): ~90 million cumulative registered users across 50+ countries and ~8 million monthly active users as of March 2024; ~130 million OCR searches per month; 7 million MAU reported Dec 2020 rising to 9.8 million monthly users by a later count; ~$130 million raised cumulatively including a $50M Series C (2021) with investors including Google, GGV Capital and SoftBank Ventures Asia. Indonesia-specific: 2.5 million users claimed by Mathpresso, equated to ~10% of SD-SMA students with smartphone access — this figure dates from November 2020 and no refreshed Indonesia-specific count was found, so it is stale and likely materially understates or misstates current usage. Independent academic evidence base is thin: one Indonesian qualitative study (GURUKU: Jurnal Pendidikan dan Sosial Humaniora, 2025) evaluated QANDA's features and potential as a self-study math medium for SD students using literature review plus analysis of user reviews — a small, non-experimental design with no learning-outcome measurement. [uncertain]
evidence_strength: moderate — feature claims and their absences are verified against primary sources (Apple App Store listing, Mathpresso's own product page, Wikipedia), which makes the negative finding on error-type diagnosis and parent dashboards reliable. Scale figures are company-reported press-release numbers with no independent audit, and the Indonesia 2.5M figure is nearly six years old. The one directly on-point academic source (Indonesian SD self-study evaluation) is qualitative and small. Contradicting SEO blog claims about a parent dashboard are weak/anecdotal and were traceable to no primary source.
remediation_efficacy_evidence: None found. No RCT, quasi-experiment, or controlled study was located showing that QANDA use improves math learning outcomes, and none showing that any diagnostic output of QANDA leads to effective remediation — unsurprising given that QANDA does not claim error-type diagnosis in the first place. Mathpresso publishes engagement and scale metrics (users, searches, speed-to-answer) rather than learning-gain evidence. The available Indonesian scholarship points the other way, raising concerns that instant-answer AI use can depress critical thinking and foster answer-copying dependence, though these are qualitative/argumentative rather than experimental findings. This is itself a competitive opening: the incumbent with 2.5M+ Indonesian users has no efficacy evidence to defend.
